newsitem.title: USA: Clinton takes hit over Iraq confusion.
newsitem.headline: Clinton takes hit over Iraq confusion.

text.p: Confusion over sending U.S. troops to Kuwait to back up the fist being shaken at Baghdad has opened President Bill Clinton to political attack and shown up the weakness of the anti-Iraq coalition.

The disarray allowed Clinton's Republican presidential opponent, Bob Dole, to score points against the president over his leadership in the current crisis and his ability to hold together the coalition formed to fight the 1991 Gulf War.

Tension between Washington and Baghdad after President Saddam Hussein's forces marched into Kurdish areas of northern Iraq two weeks ago appears to be easing despite a continued build-up of U.S. forces in the region.

Although Clinton's initial handling of the crisis, in which he ordered two salvos of cruise missiles fired at Iraqi military targets, scored well with the American people, subsequent uncertainty over policy has opened him to attack.

Last week U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry raised eyebrows in the White House when he said any response to Iraq's firing of missiles at U.S. jets would be "disproportionate." Some Clinton aides had cautioned against talking up the potential retaliation.

But the most confusion has surrounded the decision to send extra troops to Kuwait. News of the reinforcement came out in a Pentagon statement last Friday evening that 5,000 troops "will be deployed this weekend" from a U.S. base to Kuwait.

Kuwait, which had apparently not been consulted, took two days before it formally endorsed the proposal, raising questions about the commitment of the very country that Washington said it was deploying the forces to protect.
Diplomatic scurrying, including a tour of the region by Perry, did something to restore ruffled feelings, but Clinton conceded the diplomatic blunder.

"What happened was that the decision on the movements that we had made actually became public before we had done our regular consultation and the Kuwaitis had done their regular review," he told reporters on Sunday.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns at least partly blamed the media, which filled talk shows and commentary columns over weekend analysing apparently contradictory signs on just how Washington would respond to Saddam.
"I think this story was overwritten," Burns told reporters on Monday. "(We've) had a number of newspapers and wire services running that the Kuwaitis had rejected this. Absolutely untrue," he said.

Kuwait, after an embarassing 48-hour delay, allowed Clinton to send 3,000 U.S. Army ground troops from Ft. Hood, Texas to join 1,200 already there in training exercises aimed at forestalling any move by Saddam against Kuwait.
Otherwise, Perry appeared to have little to show for his weekend trip. Saudi Arabia, the major U.S. ally in the region, remained pointedly silent on its view of U.S intentions.

Other Arab nations, including Jordan and Egypt, usually friendly to Washington, have sharply criticised U.S. attacks against Iraq. Aside from Britain, Clinton has drawn no major ally to its side in the dispute with Saddam.
In the United States, Dole's Republican camp, after initially wary of attacking the president during a national security crisis, quickly took the gloves off.
House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich said White House public relations caused the blunder with Kuwait.

"We can't even get the ally we're defending to agree to be defended before we issue the press release saying we're going to be defending them. It tells you there's a certain lack of coordination. This should not be a public relations campaign," Gingrich told reporters in Marietta, Georgia.
"The president owes the country a clear explanation of what he is doing, why he is doing it and what does he hope to accomplish," Gingrich said.

Recalling President George Bush's achievement in cobbling together a 32-nation coalition in 1990 to oust Iraqi forces from Kuwait, Clinton critics say his foreign policy ineptitude has allowed the coalition to disintegrate.
Influential Arizona Republican Senator John McCain said on ABC's "This Week With David Brinkley" programme that "this situation is in terrible disarray."
"We should rebuild the coalition, which has clearly crumbled to the point where even the Kuwaitis are putting on hold the dispatch" of U.S. troops, McCain said.
